name: Besan Chilla

ingredients.name: Gram flour (besan)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ cup, lightly spooned and levelled (a scant ½ cup)

ingredients.name: Onion (pyaz/kanda)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small onion, finely chopped (about ⅓ cup)

ingredients.name: Tomato (tamatar)
ingredients.householdMeasure: ½ small tomato, deseeded and finely chopped (about ¼ cup)

ingredients.name: Groundnut oil (or any neutral cooking oil)

equipment: Flat non-stick tawa or 9–10-inch non-stick frying pan
Mixing bowl (a deep steel bowl or large mug works)
Flat spatula (wide and thin is easiest for flipping)
Measuring spoons and a measuring cup (normal teaspoons and a 200 ml steel glass are fine stand-ins)
Small bowl or brush for the oil (a teaspoon works)

steps.title: Chop the onion
steps.text: Peel and finely chop 40 g (½ small) onion.
steps.tip: Chop very fine. Big pieces make holes and the chilla tears when flipped.
steps.visualCue: Tiny, even pieces about the size of a rice grain.
steps.cameraCheck: About ⅓ cup chopped onion on the board
steps.videoShot: The knife rocking through the onion.

steps.title: Chop the tomato
steps.text: Cut ½ small tomato (40 g), scoop out the seeds and juice with a spoon, then finely chop the flesh.
steps.tip: Removing the wet seeds keeps the batter from turning watery and the chilla from going soggy.
steps.visualCue: Small red cubes, no loose seeds or juice.
steps.videoShot: The spoon scraping out seeds, then the knife dicing.

steps.title: Chop the chilli and coriander
steps.text: Finely chop ½–1 green chilli (3 g) and 1 tbsp (5 g) coriander leaves.
steps.visualCue: Fine green flecks in two small heaps
steps.cameraCheck: The chilli and coriander side by side
steps.videoShot: Coriander being chopped.

steps.title: Grate the ginger
steps.text: Peel and grate ½ tsp (3 g) ginger.
steps.visualCue: A small heap of moist, pale pulp
steps.cameraCheck: ½ tsp grated ginger on a spoon
steps.videoShot: Ginger rubbed on the fine side of the grater.

steps.title: Measure the besan
steps.text: Spoon 50 g (a scant ½ cup) besan into the bowl and level it.
steps.tip: Spoon the flour into the cup instead of scooping, or you will pack in too much.
steps.visualCue: A small mound of pale-yellow flour
steps.videoShot: Besan tipped into the bowl.

steps.title: Add the dry spices
steps.text: Add ¼ tsp ajwain (crushed between your palms), ⅛ tsp turmeric, ¼ tsp Kashmiri chilli powder and ¼ tsp salt. Stir with a spoon.
steps.visualCue: The flour turns evenly light yellow with red and green-brown specks.
steps.videoShot: Ajwain rubbed between palms and falling into the bowl.

steps.title: Add half the water
steps.text: Pour in about 50 ml (¼ cup) water.
steps.visualCue: A thick, lumpy paste
steps.videoShot: Water poured into the flour.

steps.title: Whisk out the lumps
steps.text: Whisk the thick paste hard until smooth.
steps.tip: Whisking while the paste is thick breaks lumps much faster than whisking a thin batter.
steps.visualCue: A smooth, thick paste with no dry pockets or lumps.
steps.cameraCheck: The whisk lifted out of the smooth paste
steps.videoShot: The whisk beating in fast circles.

steps.title: Thin the batter
steps.text: Add the remaining 30–40 ml water a tablespoon at a time, whisking after each, until the batter flows off the spoon in a steady ribbon.
steps.tip: Besan varies, so stop adding water as soon as it pours easily. Too thick = raw, doughy centre; too thin = it will not hold together.
steps.visualCue: Like thin pancake batter or dosa batter; it coats the back of a spoon and drips off freely.
steps.cameraCheck: Batter falling from a lifted spoon
steps.videoShot: A ribbon of batter falling back into the bowl.

steps.title: Add the vegetables
steps.text: Stir in the onion, tomato, green chilli, ginger and coriander.
steps.visualCue: Vegetables spread evenly through the yellow batter.
steps.videoShot: The spoon folding in the vegetables.

steps.title: Rest the batter (optional)
steps.text: Leave the batter for 5 min while the tawa heats.
steps.tip: If it thickens too much after resting, whisk in 1 tsp water.
steps.visualCue: The batter thickens slightly as the flour soaks up water.
steps.videoShot: (none needed)

steps.title: Heat the tawa
steps.text: Put the tawa on medium heat. Add ½ tsp oil and spread it with a spoon or folded kitchen paper.
steps.visualCue: A few drops of water flicked on the tawa sizzle and vanish in 2–3 seconds.
steps.videoShot: The oil being spread over the tawa.

steps.title: Pour the first chilla
steps.text: Stir the batter once (vegetables sink). Pour half the batter (about one ladle and a half) into the centre of the tawa.
steps.visualCue: A round puddle of batter with vegetables visible.
steps.videoShot: The batter hitting the hot tawa.

steps.title: Spread it
steps.text: Using the back of the ladle, spread the batter outward in gentle circles to about 7 inches across.
steps.tip: Do not press hard. If the tawa is too hot the batter sticks to the ladle; lower the heat a little.
steps.visualCue: An even round, a little thicker than a dosa; no gaps.
steps.videoShot: The ladle spiralling outwards.

steps.title: Drizzle oil
steps.text: Drizzle ½ tsp oil around the edge and a few drops on top.
steps.visualCue: The oil sizzles at the edges.
steps.videoShot: Oil dripping off the spoon around the edge.

steps.title: Cook the first side
steps.text: Leave it on medium heat, untouched.
steps.tip: Flipping too early is the main reason chillas break. Wait until the edges lift on their own.
steps.visualCue: The top turns from wet and glossy to dull and dry-looking; the edges lift and turn golden.
steps.cameraCheck: A spatula lifting the edge to show a golden underside
steps.videoShot: Close-up of the top going from shiny to matte.

steps.title: Flip it
steps.text: Slide the spatula fully under the chilla and flip it in one quick move.
steps.visualCue: Golden-brown underside with darker spots on the onions.
steps.cameraCheck: The flipped chilla showing the golden side
steps.videoShot: The flip.

steps.title: Cook the second side
steps.text: Press lightly with the spatula and cook.
steps.visualCue: Brown spots on the second side; the chilla feels firm, not soft, when pressed in the centre.
steps.cameraCheck: The second side lifted on the spatula
steps.videoShot: The spatula pressing the chilla gently.

steps.title: Plate the first chilla
steps.text: Fold it in half or slide it flat onto a plate.
steps.visualCue: Golden, slightly crisp edges, soft centre, no raw wet patches.
steps.cameraCheck: The first chilla on the plate
steps.videoShot: The chilla sliding onto the plate.

steps.title: Re-oil the tawa
steps.text: Lower the heat for a moment, add ½ tsp oil and spread it.
steps.tip: Letting the tawa cool slightly before the second pour helps the batter spread instead of setting in lumps.
steps.visualCue: A thin, even film of oil.
steps.videoShot: Oil spread with a paper towel.

steps.title: Make the second chilla
steps.text: Turn the heat back to medium. Stir the remaining batter, then repeat steps 13–19 (pour, spread, drizzle ½ tsp oil, cook 2–2.5 min, flip, cook 1.5–2 min).
steps.visualCue: Same as the first: golden, set, no raw centre.
steps.videoShot: The second chilla flipped.

steps.title: Serve
steps.text: Serve hot, folded or stacked, with green chutney or ketchup on the side.
steps.visualCue: Two golden rounds dotted with red, white and green vegetables.
steps.videoShot: A slow pan across the plate as a piece is torn off.

reasons: besan gives about 11 g of plant protein and 5 g of fibre in 50 g, with a lower glycaemic load than refined-flour breakfasts, and the dish is shallow-cooked in only 2 tsp oil with onion, tomato and herbs folded in. It is naturally gluten-free and vegan. Points come off because the vegetable amount is small, protein is modest for a full meal on its own, and sodium is about 600 mg. Restaurant and street versions are often brushed with butter or extra oil (e.g. "Butter Cheela" listings), salted more heavily and served with sweet ketchup or mayonnaise-based dips.

researchRating.basis: besan chilla is a hugely popular everyday North Indian breakfast, widely featured as a quick, healthy, high-protein, vegan "eggless omelette". Recipe pages score very high (Hebbar's Kitchen besan chilla / veg omelette shown at 5/5 from 268 votes in search results; Vegrecipesofindia 4.59/5 from 31 votes; Mrishtanna 5/5 from 14 votes), and nutrition sites like HealthifyMe list it as a go-to weight-loss breakfast. Small deductions because it is seen as a plain everyday dish rather than a treat, and because people often report chillas sticking, breaking or tasting raw if the batter or heat is wrong.

storage: Best eaten fresh; chillas go limp as they cool. Cooked chillas keep in an airtight box in the fridge for up to 1 day (stack them with butter paper between them). Freezing is not recommended; they turn rubbery. Reheat on a hot dry tawa for about 30–40 sec per side until warm and the edges crisp again. The uncooked batter (without tomato) keeps in the fridge for 1 day; add the tomato just before cooking.
leftoverRemix: Chilla kathi roll. Warm a leftover chilla on the tawa, spread 1 tsp green chutney, add a few strips of onion, cucumber and 2 tbsp crumbled paneer or leftover sabzi, sprinkle chaat masala, roll tightly and wrap the bottom half in butter paper. A quick, eggless "frankie" for the lunchbox.
burnOff: about 4.4 km of running (305 ÷ 70 kcal/km, for a 70 kg adult), or about 6.1 km of brisk walking (about 1 hr 15 min at 5 km/h, using about 50 kcal/km for walking) (est.).
